definition: The board outline defines the physical perimeter of the PCB used for placement, routing, mechanical checks, and fabrication data.
A copper layer is a conductive PCB layer used to form traces, pads, planes, and zones.
A dielectric layer is an insulating PCB material layer that separates conductors and influences electrical and mechanical behavior.
A PCB stackup is the ordered top-to-bottom definition of conductive and dielectric layers, thicknesses, materials, and sourced properties.
Relative permittivity describes how a dielectric material stores electric-field energy compared with vacuum and is an important input to impedance analysis.
Loss tangent quantifies dielectric energy loss and is an important material input for frequency-dependent signal-loss analysis.
A trace is a routed copper conductor that electrically connects points on the same PCB layer.
Trace width is the physical width of a routed copper conductor and must satisfy the applicable geometry and current requirements.
A via is a plated hole or structure that electrically connects copper features on different PCB layers.
Via drill is the diameter of the drilled or formed hole associated with a through, blind, buried, or other supported via type.
An annular ring is the radial copper width surrounding a drilled hole or via barrel on a conductive layer.
Clearance is the minimum allowed physical spacing between specified conductive or mechanical PCB features under a defined rule.
A copper zone is a filled conductive region typically assigned to a net for power distribution, grounding, shielding, or thermal purposes.
A plane is a broad conductive region or layer used as a low-impedance reference, power distribution structure, or return path.
A keepout is a board region that prohibits selected objects such as copper, traces, vias, components, or routing from entering it.
A mechanical object represents non-electrical board geometry such as cutouts, dimensions, mounting features, or enclosure constraints.
Current load is the caller-supplied current assigned to a trace for comparison with an independently sourced current limit.
A trace current limit is a sourced maximum current value used for validation under the conditions that produced that limit.
Controlled impedance is a design requirement that constrains a routed interconnect to a specified characteristic impedance within a defined tolerance.
Single-ended impedance is the characteristic impedance of one signal conductor referenced to its return structure.
Differential impedance is the impedance seen by the opposing signal currents of a defined differential pair.
A differential pair is a matched pair of conductors intended to carry equal and opposite signal components with controlled geometry and coupling.
A return path is the conductive route taken by signal return current relative to its outgoing signal path.
A return-path discontinuity is a gap, transition, or interruption that forces return current away from its intended reference route.
A microvia is a small fabricated via, commonly laser formed, used for high-density interconnection between selected adjacent or nearby layers.
Via in pad is a PCB construction technique that places a via directly within a component pad and may require specialized filling or capping.
BGA fanout is the routing and via strategy used to escape signals from the dense pad field of a ball-grid-array package.
